VIDEO.title: What REALLY Shocked Jesus About the Centurion's Faith? (Matthew 8:1-17)
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 8:1-17. Jesus comes down from the mountain and heals three people: a leper, a centurion's paralyzed servant, and Peter's mother-in-law. That evening He heals many more, fulfilling Isaiah. Parallels: Mark 1:29-34, 40-45 and Luke 4:38-41.

All three are outcasts of a sort: the leper is ritually unclean, the centurion is a Gentile and part of the occupying power, and Peter's mother-in-law is a woman in a world where women had lower status.

Each healing is Jesus living out His sermon. He tells the leper to obey Leviticus 14 (5:17, not abolishing the Law) and to tell no one (6:1, not practicing righteousness to be seen). He honors a Roman officer's request (5:43-48, love your enemies; 5:41, the extra mile).

'Many will come from east and west' is a hint (remez) of Psalm 107 and Isaiah 65: Gentiles who cry out to the Lord will sit at God's banquet, while 'sons of the kingdom' who forsake Him are cast out, as in 7:21-23.

Jesus marvels at the centurion. With D. A. Carson, the video says the wonder is not just that he believed Jesus could heal from a distance, but how deeply he grasped the secret of Jesus' authority: illness obeys Jesus as soldiers obey an officer.

The lesson: the kind of heart a disciple has gives unique spiritual insight, even discernment, about Jesus. The centurion's humility ('I am not good enough') is the poor-in-spirit heart of the Beatitudes. What qualities of heart are we cultivating?
QUOTES: Jesus comes down from the mountain and does three things that would absolutely shock any Torah observant Jew.
Like any good rabbi, he knew that abstract concepts need concrete examples.
The kind of heart a disciple has provides unique spiritual insights, dare I say discernment about Jesus.
If Jesus tells health itself to go do something, it does it immediately.

method.p: The teacher's tip: read Matthew's account, then the same events in Mark 1:29-34, 40-45 and Luke 4:38-41 (and the centurion in Luke 7:1-10). The other Gospels add details that color in the scene.

LSB_QUOTES.text: Lord, I am not good enough for You to come under my roof, but just say the word, and my servant will be healed.
Truly I say to you, I have not found such great faith with anyone in Israel.
He Himself took our infirmities and carried away our diseases.

src.text: And behold, a leper came to Him and was bowing down before Him, and said, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” And Jesus stretched out His hand and touched him, saying, “I am willing; be cleansed.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed.

left.text: He shall live alone; his place of habitation shall be outside the camp.

right.text: Am I God, to put to death and to make alive, that this man is sending word to me to cure a man of his leprosy?

lines.text: The leper is an outcast through bodily and ritual uncleanness, yet he is convinced Jesus has the authority to heal him. Healing leprosy was thought as hard as raising the dead (2 Kings 5:7). This is the first detailed healing in Matthew.
No Israelite leper had been healed by a prophet: 'none of them was cleansed, but only Naaman the Syrian' (Luke 4:27), and Naaman was not healed directly.
Chrysostom on the touch: 'His hand became not unclean from the leprosy, but the leprous body was rendered clean by His holy hand' (Homilies on Matthew 25).

src.text: But the centurion said, “Lord, I am not good enough for You to come under my roof, but just say the word, and my servant will be healed. For I also am a man under authority, with soldiers under me; and I say to this man, ‘Go!’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come!’ and he comes, and to my slave, ‘Do this!’ and he does it.”

lines.text: A Gentile, an enemy officer, believes healing can happen at a distance. Others came close to Jesus to be healed; the centurion saw that Jesus' authority was not limited by distance. How he worked this out, Scripture does not say.
He uses his own authority as an analogy: illness, health and even the body are soldiers under Jesus' command. If Jesus tells health to go, it goes.
Luke's account adds that Jewish elders pleaded for him: 'he loves our nation and it was he who built us our synagogue' (Luke 7:5).

HEALS.title: She got up and served Him

src.text: When Jesus came into Peter’s home, He saw his mother-in-law lying sick in bed with a fever. And He touched her hand, and the fever left her; and she got up and began waiting on Him.

lines.text: Touching her hand broke the social norms of the day, and Mark's account places it on the Sabbath (Mark 1:21, 29-31). That may be why the crowds waited until evening (8:16): they were waiting for the Sabbath to end.
She 'began waiting on Him' (diakoneō, in a tense that can mean 'kept serving'), the word often used for Christian service. Some see a sign that she became a disciple.
Peter had a home in Capernaum, and a wife (1 Corinthians 9:5). Excavators have found a first-century house under a later church there, traditionally Peter's.

src.text: Now when evening came, they brought to Him many who were demon-possessed; and He cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were ill in order to fulfill what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, “He Himself took our infirmities and carried away our diseases.”

right.text: Surely our griefs He Himself bore, / And our sorrows He carried;

lines.text: Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4 closer to the Hebrew, where the words also mean 'sicknesses' and 'pains.' Healing the sick fulfills the Servant's work; 'with a word' echoes the centurion's 'just say the word.'

LIVED.title: Go, show yourself to the priest

left.text: Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill.

right.text: go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them.

lines.text: Jesus tells the healed man to fulfill the Torah's law of cleansing (Leviticus 14). He is not abolishing the Law.

LIVED.title: See that you tell no one

left.text: Beware of doing your righteousness before men to be noticed by them;

right.text: See that you tell no one;

lines.text: He does a great deed and asks for silence: righteousness that is not done to be seen.
Chrysostom: 'He bids him tell no man, teaching us to avoid boasting and vainglory' (Homilies on Matthew 25).

LIVED.title: I will come and heal him

left.text: But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,

right.text: I will come and heal him.

lines.text: Romans were Gentiles, pagans and the occupying enemy. Jesus greets one and honors his request. 'Love' here is agapaō: seek your enemy's good, even giving up your own rights.
The 'one mile' of 5:41 fits Roman soldiers, who could force a local to carry gear for a mile. Now Jesus shows what loving such a man looks like.

LIVED.title: Sons of the kingdom cast out

left.text: I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness.

right.text: but the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness; in that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

lines.text: These are not lifelong unbelievers but 'sons of the kingdom' who should know better. The disciples should connect this with the warning of 7:21-23.

TABLE.title: From the east and from the west

left.text: And gathered from the lands, / From the east and from the west, / From the north and from the south.

right.text: Then they cried out to Yahweh in their trouble; / He delivered them out of their distresses.

lines.text: Those who cry out to the Lord, even non-Jews, will be delivered; the refrain repeats (107:13).
Added: the same psalm says, 'He sent His word and healed them' (Psalm 107:20), a striking parallel to 'just say the word.'

src.text: But you who forsake Yahweh, / Who forget My holy mountain, / Who set a table for Fortune, / ... Behold, My slaves will eat, but you will be hungry.

lines.text: The ones who forsake the Lord find they are not welcome at God's table. A hard idea for Jesus' hearers: Gentiles welcomed, sons of the kingdom cast out.

src.text: And Yahweh of hosts will prepare a lavish banquet for all peoples on this mountain;

lines.text: Added: the prophets pictured the end-time feast with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as open to all peoples. 'Recline' (anaklinō) is the posture of a formal meal.

src.text: but the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness; in that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

lines.text: A picture Jesus repeats throughout His ministry; the video says it comes from Old Testament passages and will return to it later.
The same phrase comes back in 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30. Compare 'They gnash their teeth' at the righteous (Psalm 112:10).

PEOPLE.name: Jesus
PEOPLE.video: Comes down from the mountain and walks out His own sermon: He keeps the Law, avoids being seen, loves an enemy, and marvels at a Gentile's insight.
PEOPLE.bg: Matthew 8-9 gathers ten miracles after the sermon: Jesus is Messiah in word (5-7) and deed (8-9).

PEOPLE.name: The leper
PEOPLE.video: An outcast, unclean, who believes Jesus can make him clean if He is willing.
PEOPLE.bg: Lepers had to live alone outside the camp and cry 'Unclean!' (Leviticus 13:45-46).

PEOPLE.name: The centurion
PEOPLE.video: A Gentile officer, and part of the occupation. Humble ('not good enough'), and he understands Jesus' authority.
PEOPLE.bg: A centurion commanded about 80-100 soldiers. In Capernaum he may have served Herod Antipas rather than Rome directly; Luke says he built the synagogue (Luke 7:5).

PEOPLE.name: Peter's mother-in-law
PEOPLE.video: Healed by Jesus' touch; she serves Him, perhaps as a new disciple.
PEOPLE.bg: The only member of Peter's family named in the Gospels besides his brother Andrew.

PEOPLE.name: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
PEOPLE.video: The patriarchs at the banquet table, joined by many from east and west.
PEOPLE.bg: God's promise to Abraham: 'in you all the families of the earth will be blessed' (Genesis 12:3).

PEOPLE.name: Isaiah
PEOPLE.video: Quoted by Matthew: 'He Himself took our infirmities.'
PEOPLE.bg: Isaiah 53 is the fourth Servant Song.

PEOPLE.name: Naaman
PEOPLE.video: The Syrian leper healed in Elisha's day, not a Jew and not touched by the prophet.
PEOPLE.bg: Elisha sent a messenger: 'Go and wash in the Jordan seven times' (2 Kings 5:10).

TERMS.def: In the Bible, a range of skin diseases, not only Hansen's disease. It made a person ritually unclean (Leviticus 13-14).
An officer over a 'century' of roughly 80-100 soldiers.
Hebrew for one of illegitimate birth (Deuteronomy 23:2), barred from the assembly. The video uses it for outsiders in general.
A 'hint' that calls an Old Testament passage to mind: here, Psalm 107 and Isaiah 65.
To love by seeking another's good, even at your own cost (5:44).
Those who by birth expected a place in the kingdom (8:12).
A picture of exclusion from the lit banquet hall; with 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' it describes final judgment.
About the last things: the end of the age and the final judgment (8:11-12).

WORDS.gloss: Servant, or child; Luke calls him a slave (doulos).
To serve, wait on; root of 'deacon.'

BACKGROUND.p: Leviticus 13-14 describes how a priest examined skin disease and later declared a healed person clean, with offerings. A leper lived outside the camp. Touching one made a person unclean.
Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas, whose troops were organized on Roman lines and included non-Jews. Matthew does not say 'Roman'; either way he was a Gentile officer of the ruling power.
Under an octagonal Byzantine church in Capernaum, archaeologists found a first-century house that early Christians seem to have honored as Peter's.
Mark sets these events on a Sabbath (Mark 1:21-32). The Sabbath ended at sunset, so people could carry the sick after evening came.

WITNESSES.text: For His hand became not unclean from the leprosy, but the leprous body was rendered clean by His holy hand.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 25, on 8:3. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: For he did no less than imagine to himself, as it seems to me, the armies in Heaven; or that the diseases and death, and everything else, were so subject to Him, as his soldiers to himself.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 26, on 8:9. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: Having therefore touched her body, He not only quenched the fever, but also gave her back perfect health.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 27, on 8:15. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

DEBATES.h: Why tell the leper to tell no one?
DEBATES.p: The video: Jesus lives out 6:1. Others: to avoid crowds seeking only miracles (Mark 1:45 shows what happened), or to let the priest's verdict be the 'testimony to them.' Chrysostom: to teach us to avoid boasting.
The video, following D. A. Carson: the depth of the centurion's insight into Jesus' authority, not just the size of his trust.
Matthew has him speak to Jesus; Luke says he sent Jewish elders and friends (Luke 7:3, 6). Many explain this as a common way of speaking: acting through agents counts as acting in person.
Women had fewer legal rights, and some later rabbinic sayings discourage talking with women. Practice varied, and women supported Jesus' ministry (Luke 8:1-3).

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: 'You who forsake Yahweh, who forget My holy mountain' is Isaiah 65:11 (the captions say 65:1); 'I will destine you for the sword' is 65:12.

In Deuteronomy 23 the mamzer ('illegitimate birth') is in verse 2; the Ammonites and Moabites are a separate law (verse 3), and 'never seek their peace or their prosperity' (verse 6) is about them, not about the mamzer.
Mark and Luke parallel the leper and the fever (Mark 1:29-34, 40-45; Luke 4:38-41; 5:12-16), but the centurion's parallel is Luke 7:1-10, not in Mark.
Matthew does not say the centurion was Roman. In Galilee he may have served Herod Antipas; either way he was a Gentile officer.
The video quotes D. A. Carson without a citation. The idea, that the centurion grasped the secret of Jesus' authority, is the video's summary of Carson; the exact words could not be checked.

QUESTIONS: Who are the 'outcasts' in your world? What would it look like to touch them, as Jesus did?
Jesus lived out His teaching right after giving it. Which recent teaching could you live out this week?
The centurion said, 'I am not good enough.' How does humility open our eyes to who Jesus is?
What does it mean to you that sickness obeys Jesus like a soldier?
Is there an 'enemy' whose good you could seek, as Jesus did for the centurion?
The video asks: are the qualities of heart in our churches in line with the Beatitudes? Gut check: what about yours?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The lesson for the original audience: the kind of heart a disciple has provides unique spiritual insight, even discernment, about Jesus. The centurion's humble, poor-in-spirit character gave him insight that the scribes and Pharisees lacked, though they obeyed the Law. This kind of heart will bring Gentiles to God's banquet and exclude the sons of the kingdom. For us: what qualities of heart are we cultivating in ourselves and our churches? Are they in line with the Beatitudes? Think about how it applies directly to your life so that you can do something about it.
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): pray the centurion's words this week: 'Lord, I am not good enough... but just say the word' (8:8). Bring one person who cannot come to Jesus on their own, as the centurion did for his servant, and ask on their behalf.

   [Background] Luke's account adds that Jewish elders pleaded for him: 'he loves our nation and it was he who built us our synagogue' (Luke 7:5). (Luke 7:1-10)
3. Peter's mother-in-law · Matthew 8:14-15: She got up and served Him
   Serve Matthew 8:14-15: "When Jesus came into Peter’s home, He saw his mother-in-law lying sick in bed with a fever. And He touched her hand, and the fever left her; and she got up and began waiting on Him." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+8:14-15
   (video) Touching her hand broke the social norms of the day, and Mark's account places it on the Sabbath (Mark 1:21, 29-31). That may be why the crowds waited until evening (8:16): they were waiting for the Sabbath to end. (Mark 1:21; Mark 1:29-34)
   (video) She 'began waiting on Him' (diakoneō, in a tense that can mean 'kept serving'), the word often used for Christian service. Some see a sign that she became a disciple.
   [Background] Peter had a home in Capernaum, and a wife (1 Corinthians 9:5). Excavators have found a first-century house under a later church there, traditionally Peter's. (1 Corinthians 9:5)
4. That evening · Matthew 8:16-17: He took our infirmities
   Isaiah (Isaiah 53:4, LSB): "Surely our griefs He Himself bore, / And our sorrows He carried;"
   Isaiah Matthew 8:16-17: "Now when evening came, they brought to Him many who were demon-possessed; and He cast out the spirits with a word, and healed all who were ill in order to fulfill what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet, saying, “He Himself took our infirmities and carried away our diseases.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+8:16-17
   [Background] Matthew quotes Isaiah 53:4 closer to the Hebrew, where the words also mean 'sicknesses' and 'pains.' Healing the sick fulfills the Servant's work; 'with a word' echoes the centurion's 'just say the word.'

## The sermon lived out
1. Not to abolish · 5:17 and 8:4: Go, show yourself to the priest
   The sermon (Matthew 5:17, LSB): "Do not think that I came to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I did not come to abolish but to fulfill."
   Down the mountain (Matthew 8:4, LSB): "go, show yourself to the priest and present the offering that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them."
   (video) Jesus tells the healed man to fulfill the Torah's law of cleansing (Leviticus 14). He is not abolishing the Law. (Leviticus 14:2-4)
2. Not to be seen · 6:1 and 8:4: See that you tell no one
   The sermon (Matthew 6:1, LSB): "Beware of doing your righteousness before men to be noticed by them;"
   Down the mountain (Matthew 8:4, LSB): "See that you tell no one;"
   (video) He does a great deed and asks for silence: righteousness that is not done to be seen.
   [Background] Chrysostom: 'He bids him tell no man, teaching us to avoid boasting and vainglory' (Homilies on Matthew 25).
3. Love your enemies · 5:44 and 8:7: I will come and heal him
   The sermon (Matthew 5:44, LSB): "But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,"
   Down the mountain (Matthew 8:7, LSB): "I will come and heal him."
   (video) Romans were Gentiles, pagans and the occupying enemy. Jesus greets one and honors his request. 'Love' here is agapaō: seek your enemy's good, even giving up your own rights.
   (video) The 'one mile' of 5:41 fits Roman soldiers, who could force a local to carry gear for a mile. Now Jesus shows what loving such a man looks like. (Matthew 5:41)
4. Lord, Lord · 7:22-23 and 8:12: Sons of the kingdom cast out
   The sermon (Matthew 7:23, LSB): "I never knew you; depart from Me, you who practice lawlessness."
   Down the mountain (Matthew 8:12, LSB): "but the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness; in that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth."
   (video) These are not lifelong unbelievers but 'sons of the kingdom' who should know better. The disciples should connect this with the warning of 7:21-23.

## Many from east and west
1. Remez · Psalm 107: From the east and from the west
   The gathering (Psalm 107:3, LSB): "And gathered from the lands, / From the east and from the west, / From the north and from the south."
   The refrain (Psalm 107:6, LSB): "Then they cried out to Yahweh in their trouble; / He delivered them out of their distresses."
   (video) Those who cry out to the Lord, even non-Jews, will be delivered; the refrain repeats (107:13). (Psalm 107:13)
   [Background] Added: the same psalm says, 'He sent His word and healed them' (Psalm 107:20), a striking parallel to 'just say the word.' (Psalm 107:20)
2. Remez · Isaiah 65: Who forget My holy mountain
   Forsake Isaiah 65:11-13: "But you who forsake Yahweh, / Who forget My holy mountain, / Who set a table for Fortune, / ... Behold, My slaves will eat, but you will be hungry." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Isaiah+65:11-13
   (video) The ones who forsake the Lord find they are not welcome at God's table. A hard idea for Jesus' hearers: Gentiles welcomed, sons of the kingdom cast out.
3. Background · Isaiah 25:6: A banquet for all peoples
   Feast Isaiah 25:6: "And Yahweh of hosts will prepare a lavish banquet for all peoples on this mountain;" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Isaiah+25:6
   [Background] Added: the prophets pictured the end-time feast with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as open to all peoples. 'Recline' (anaklinō) is the posture of a formal meal.
4. Outer darkness: Weeping and gnashing of teeth
   Judgment Matthew 8:12: "but the sons of the kingdom will be cast out into the outer darkness; in that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+8:12
   (video) A picture Jesus repeats throughout His ministry; the video says it comes from Old Testament passages and will return to it later.
   [Background] The same phrase comes back in 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30. Compare 'They gnash their teeth' at the righteous (Psalm 112:10). (Matthew 22:13; Matthew 25:30)

## Key people
- Jesus: Comes down from the mountain and walks out His own sermon: He keeps the Law, avoids being seen, loves an enemy, and marvels at a Gentile's insight. [Background] Matthew 8-9 gathers ten miracles after the sermon: Jesus is Messiah in word (5-7) and deed (8-9).
- The leper: An outcast, unclean, who believes Jesus can make him clean if He is willing. [Background] Lepers had to live alone outside the camp and cry 'Unclean!' (Leviticus 13:45-46).
- The centurion: A Gentile officer, and part of the occupation. Humble ('not good enough'), and he understands Jesus' authority. [Background] A centurion commanded about 80-100 soldiers. In Capernaum he may have served Herod Antipas rather than Rome directly; Luke says he built the synagogue (Luke 7:5).
- Peter's mother-in-law: Healed by Jesus' touch; she serves Him, perhaps as a new disciple. [Background] The only member of Peter's family named in the Gospels besides his brother Andrew.
- Abraham, Isaac and Jacob: The patriarchs at the banquet table, joined by many from east and west. [Background] God's promise to Abraham: 'in you all the families of the earth will be blessed' (Genesis 12:3).
- Isaiah: Quoted by Matthew: 'He Himself took our infirmities.' [Background] Isaiah 53 is the fourth Servant Song.
- Naaman: The Syrian leper healed in Elisha's day, not a Jew and not touched by the prophet. [Background] Elisha sent a messenger: 'Go and wash in the Jordan seven times' (2 Kings 5:10).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum (named in the video): Where the centurion meets Jesus (8:5), and Peter's home (8:14).
- Mount of Beatitudes: Traditional site of the sermon: 'when Jesus came down from the mountain' (8:1).
- Tabgha: A spring-fed cove just west of Capernaum.
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas' capital: the centurion may have served in his forces.
- Magdala: A large fishing town on the western shore.
- Bethsaida: Peter's earlier home town (John 1:44).

## Key terms
- Leprosy: In the Bible, a range of skin diseases, not only Hansen's disease. It made a person ritually unclean (Leviticus 13-14). [Background]
- Centurion: An officer over a 'century' of roughly 80-100 soldiers.
- Mamzer: Hebrew for one of illegitimate birth (Deuteronomy 23:2), barred from the assembly. The video uses it for outsiders in general.
- Remez: A 'hint' that calls an Old Testament passage to mind: here, Psalm 107 and Isaiah 65.
- Agapaō: To love by seeking another's good, even at your own cost (5:44).
- Sons of the kingdom: Those who by birth expected a place in the kingdom (8:12).
- Outer darkness: A picture of exclusion from the lit banquet hall; with 'weeping and gnashing of teeth' it describes final judgment.
- Eschatological: About the last things: the end of the age and the final judgment (8:11-12).

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Leprosy and the Law: Leviticus 13-14 describes how a priest examined skin disease and later declared a healed person clean, with offerings. A leper lived outside the camp. Touching one made a person unclean.
- Centurions in Galilee: Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas, whose troops were organized on Roman lines and included non-Jews. Matthew does not say 'Roman'; either way he was a Gentile officer of the ruling power.
- A house in Capernaum: Under an octagonal Byzantine church in Capernaum, archaeologists found a first-century house that early Christians seem to have honored as Peter's.
- Evening and the Sabbath: Mark sets these events on a Sabbath (Mark 1:21-32). The Sabbath ended at sunset, so people could carry the sick after evening came.

## Early witnesses [Background: sourced]
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For His hand became not unclean from the leprosy, but the leprous body was rendered clean by His holy hand." Homilies on Matthew 25, on 8:3. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For he did no less than imagine to himself, as it seems to me, the armies in Heaven; or that the diseases and death, and everything else, were so subject to Him, as his soldiers to himself." Homilies on Matthew 26, on 8:9. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Having therefore touched her body, He not only quenched the fever, but also gave her back perfect health." Homilies on Matthew 27, on 8:15. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Why tell the leper to tell no one? The video: Jesus lives out 6:1. Others: to avoid crowds seeking only miracles (Mark 1:45 shows what happened), or to let the priest's verdict be the 'testimony to them.' Chrysostom: to teach us to avoid boasting.
- What amazed Jesus? The video, following D. A. Carson: the depth of the centurion's insight into Jesus' authority, not just the size of his trust.
- Did the centurion come himself? Matthew has him speak to Jesus; Luke says he sent Jewish elders and friends (Luke 7:3, 6). Many explain this as a common way of speaking: acting through agents counts as acting in person.
- Were women 'second-class citizens'? Women had fewer legal rights, and some later rabbinic sayings discourage talking with women. Practice varied, and women supported Jesus' ministry (Luke 8:1-3).

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- 'You who forsake Yahweh, who forget My holy mountain' is Isaiah 65:11 (the captions say 65:1); 'I will destine you for the sword' is 65:12.
- In Deuteronomy 23 the mamzer ('illegitimate birth') is in verse 2; the Ammonites and Moabites are a separate law (verse 3), and 'never seek their peace or their prosperity' (verse 6) is about them, not about the mamzer.
- Mark and Luke parallel the leper and the fever (Mark 1:29-34, 40-45; Luke 4:38-41; 5:12-16), but the centurion's parallel is Luke 7:1-10, not in Mark.
- Matthew does not say the centurion was Roman. In Galilee he may have served Herod Antipas; either way he was a Gentile officer.
- The video quotes D. A. Carson without a citation. The idea, that the centurion grasped the secret of Jesus' authority, is the video's summary of Carson; the exact words could not be checked.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Who are the 'outcasts' in your world? What would it look like to touch them, as Jesus did?
2. Jesus lived out His teaching right after giving it. Which recent teaching could you live out this week?
3. The centurion said, 'I am not good enough.' How does humility open our eyes to who Jesus is?
4. What does it mean to you that sickness obeys Jesus like a soldier?
5. Is there an 'enemy' whose good you could seek, as Jesus did for the centurion?
6. The video asks: are the qualities of heart in our churches in line with the Beatitudes? Gut check: what about yours?

## Application
- (video) The lesson for the original audience: the kind of heart a disciple has provides unique spiritual insight, even discernment, about Jesus. The centurion's humble, poor-in-spirit character gave him insight that the scribes and Pharisees lacked, though they obeyed the Law. This kind of heart will bring Gentiles to God's banquet and exclude the sons of the kingdom. For us: what qualities of heart are we cultivating in ourselves and our churches? Are they in line with the Beatitudes? Think about how it applies directly to your life so that you can do something about it.
- Study note (added): pray the centurion's words this week: 'Lord, I am not good enough... but just say the word' (8:8). Bring one person who cannot come to Jesus on their own, as the centurion did for his servant, and ask on their behalf.
